fetched_contents.text: (PDF) HMM-based persian speech synthesis using limited adaptation data Speech synthesis systems provided for the Persian language so far need various large-scale speech corpora to synthesize several target speakers' voice. Accordingly, synthesizing speech with a small amount of data seems to be essential in Persian. Taking advantage of a speaker adaptation in the speech synthesis systems makes it possible to generate speech with remarkable quality when the data of the speaker are limited. Here we conducted this method for the first time in Persian. This paper describes speaker adaptation based on Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) in Persian speech synthesis system for FARsi Speech DATabase (FARSDAT). In this regard, we prepared the whole FARSDAT, then for synthesizing speech with arbitrary speaker characteristics, we trained the average voice units; afterward, the adapted model was obtained by transforming the average voice model. We demonstrate that a few speech data of a target speaker are sufficient to obtain high quality synthetic speech, and we set out synthetic speech which has been generated from adapted models by using only 88 utterances is very close to that from speaker dependent models trained using 355 utterances. Discover the world's research * 25+ million members * 160+ million publication pages * 2.3+ billion citations Join for free HMM-Based Persian Speech Synthesis Using Limited Adaptation Data Fahimeh Bahmaninezhad, Hossein Sameti, Soheil Khorram Department of Computer Engineering, Sharif University of Technology, Tehran, Iran bahmaninezhad@ce.sharif.edu, sameti@sharif.edu, khorram@ce.sharif.edu Abstract — Speech synthesis systems provided for the Persian language so far need various large-scale speech corpora to synthesize several target speakers’ voice. Accordingly, synthesizing speech with a small amount of data seems to be essential in Persian. Taking advantage of a speaker adaptation in the speech synthesis systems makes it possible to generate speech with remarkable quality when the data of the speaker are limited. Here we conducted this method for the first time in Persian. This paper describes speaker adaptation based on Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) in Persian speech synthesis system for FARsi Speech DATabase (FARSDAT). In this regard, we prepared the whole FARSDAT, then for synthesizing speech with arbitrary speaker characteristics, we trained the average voice units; afterward, the adapted model was obtained by transforming the average voice model. We demonstrate that a few speech data of a target speaker are sufficient to obtain high quality synthetic speech, and we set out synthetic speech which has been generated from adapted models by using only 88 utterances is very close to that from speaker dependent models trained using 355 utterances. Keywords-component; Persian speech synthesis, average voice model, speaker adaptation, automatic annotation of FARSDAT I.I NTRODUCTION Speech synthesis is referred to a technique which converts symbolic linguistic representations into human speech. A large variety of methods have been proposed, however HMM-based approach has dominated other methods over the last ten years [1, 2]. The main problem of building a new voice is to collect and prepare a labeled speech data. It is desirable to synthesize high quality speech using a small amount of speech data. This goal is achieved by employing speaker adaptation framework [3]. In other words, the modeling strategy is chosen by considering the amount of available speech data which belongs to the target speaker. Broadly speaking, speaker-dependent framework is an appropriate choice for a large amount of speech data while, adapting the average voice model to the target speaker [3] becomes favorable when available speech data of the target speaker are limited [4]. In speaker-adaptive framework, a large variety of contextual information extracted from several speakers’ data, are utilized to build the average voice model. It provides a priori information for the speaker adaptation, and a robust basis is obtained as a result [5]. Thereby, the stable synthesized speech can be achieved even if the amount of speech data available for the target speaker is small. Speaker adaptation is an issue of interest in most speech processing applications. Speaker adaptation techniques have been used in speech recognition systems [6] for quite a long time. Then, by introducing the HMM-based speech synthesis systems, these techniques are adopted to be used for speech synthesis. Speaker-adaptive HMM-based speech synthesis was initially implemented for Japanese language [4], and later was applied to English [7-10]. In this work, it is incorporated in Persian speech synthesis. This paper describes the speaker-adaptive HMM-based speech synthesis framework for FARSDAT database [11]. FARSDAT is an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) corpus comprising utterances from 100 Persian speakers of different ages, sex, educations, and dialects. In this study, we extracted the features and contextual information of all the 100 speakers automatically, thus we could synthesize 100 speaker-adaptive HMM-based speech synthesis systems. Speech synthesis systems resulted from this work are valuable sources which can be used for further research areas such as eigenvoice conversion [12]. For generating each speaker’s synthesis system, at first we model the average voice using train data of several speakers, then the adapted model is obtained by transforming the average voice model, using adaptation data of the target speaker, and finally synthesized speech are obtained from this adapted model. fetched_contents.text: Emotional Speech Synthesis Felix Burkhardt and Nick Campbell Abstract Emotional speech synthesis is an important part of the puzzle on the long way to human-like artificial human-machine interaction. During the way, lots of stations like emotional audio messages or believable characters in gaming will be reached. This chapter discusses technical aspects of emotional speech synthesis, shows practical application and highlights new developments concerning the realization of affective speech with non-uniform unit selection based synthesis and voice transformation techniques. Keywords/keyphrases Speech synthesis, non-uniform unit-selection, hmm synthesis, voice transformation 1. Introduction No one ever speaks without emotion. Despite this fact, emotional simulation is not yet a self-evident feature in current speech synthesizers. One reason for this perhaps lies in the complexity of human vocal expression: current state-of-the-art synthesizers still struggle with the challenge of generating understandable (for domain-independent systems) and natural sounding speech, although the latter requirement in itself already indicates the importance of affective expression. This chapter gives an overview on the state of art with respect to different aspects of emotional speech synthesis, ranging from use cases and emotion models to technical approaches. For a deeper understanding of the principles of speech synthesis see (Taylor 2009), for a deeper history of emotional speech synthesis, the reader is refered to (Murray & Arnott 1993) and (Schroder 2001). 1 The notion of emotional behavior is a most imprecise and difficult one to describe. As a psychologist once famously remarked: "everyone except a psychologist knows what an emotion is" (Young 1973, cited in Kleinginna & Kleinginna 1981). Fortunately, this definition problem concerns emotion recognition much more than emotional speech synthesis, because in the former case one needs an accurate model of "the real world" in order to capture the multitude of emotional expressions, while in the latter, a simple model based on a few basic emotions might suffice for many applications, even if a "natural" expression rarely is of this form . Simulated emotional expression is typically very well recognized when limited to the display of some exaggerated prototypical emotions (Murray & Arnott 1993, Burkhardt 2000, Schroder 2001). Figure 1: General architecture for an emotional text to speech synthesis system 2 Generally speaking, speech synthesis can be classified under the following three types (although hybrid forms are possible). Voice response systems as used in a recorded announcement of stops in public transport systems., Re- or copy-synthesis as used to alter a speech signal in its voice- related features. A special case would be voice transformation, for example changing in the case of voice conversion, a speech signal from a source to a target speaker. Voice transformation techniques can be used to generate an emotional expression. Arbitrary speech synthesizers; these in contrast can process any kind of input, given the limits of a target language. It must be noted though that all synthesizers are somewhat domain restricted. They might be divided into text-to-speech vs. concept-to-speech systems, depending on the information given with the text. With respect to the topic at hand, concept-to-speech systems might be able to label text automatically with target emotions. An overall architecture of an emotional speech synthesis system is shown in Figure 1. The text to be synthesized is either given as input or generated by a text generation system. Although text generation systems are beyond the scope of this article, formalisms to annotate text emotionally are discussed in Section 4 of this chapter as well as in chapter 29 on Emotion Markup Language. A text-to-speech synthesizer converts text into speech by first analyzing the text by natural language processing (NLP) and conversion to a phonemic representation aligned with a prosodic structure, which is passed to a digital speech processing (DSP) component in order to generate a speech signal. Both of these sub modules might be influenced by the emotion modeling component. Approaches to generating emotional speech will be discussed further in Section 6. Features of the speech signal are spectral (the "sound" of the voice), prosodic (the "melody" of the speech), phonetic (kind of spoken phones, reductions and elaborations), ideolectal (choice of words) and semantic (giving the meaning). All of these can be influenced by emotional expression, although, for practical reasons, 3 speech synthesis systems typically take only a subset of these features into account. Aspects of emotional expression affecting speech features are discussed in Section 5. The component responsible for generating the emotional expression needs to be trained on a database of emotional examples, irrespective of whether rules are derived from the data or statistical algorithms are produced. Databases are often recorded by actors (Burkhardt, 2005), taken from real life data (Campbell, 2003), or from TV (Devilliers et al, 2006). From these, a rule base or model can be generated and used to control the synthesizer. All the components of the emotion processing system need to have the same emotion model as a basis. Different approaches to designate and describe emotions are discussed further in Section 3. A productive system must be evaluated by some means or other. Performance results and listening test designs will be discussed in Section 7. The quality of an emotional synthesizer of course depends primarily on its application, respectively the character appearance: a synthesizer giving cartoon figures a voice meets different demands than a system to make the voice of a speech disabled person more natural. Common adaptation techniques in HMM speech synthesis, especially when training data is limited, are centered on speaker adaptation and related state-level or model-space transformations. The foundational HMM-based speech synthesis system described in HTS Version 2.0 explicitly states that HMMs are used to model spectrum, excitation, and duration, and that the system can generate speech waveforms from the HMMs themselves [N1-F1]. It also notes that voice characteristics, speaking styles, or emotions can be modified by transforming HMM parameters using techniques such as adaptation, interpolation, eigenvoice, or multiple regression [N1-F1]. This establishes that adaptation is a core method in HMM synthesis for modifying output behavior.

For limited training data, speaker adaptation is particularly important. The Persian speech synthesis paper shows that a small amount of target speaker data can be sufficient to obtain high-quality synthetic speech and that speaker adaptation makes it possible to generate speech with remarkable quality when the speaker data are limited [N1-F2]. It further describes a pipeline in which an average voice model is trained on data from several speakers, and then the adapted model is obtained by transforming that average voice model using adaptation data from the target speaker [N1-F2]. This method directly addresses limited data by starting with a general-purpose average model and fine-tuning it with minimal target-specific data.

Cross-lingual/state-mapping techniques are another common adaptation approach. The HTS paper mentions cross-lingual speaker adaptation techniques using state mapping and notes that identical model training methods can be used across languages [N1-R4]. The cross-lingual speaker adaptation literature cited in N6 emphasizes that state mapping methods establish a mapping between source and target voice models using Kullback-Leibler divergence or other similarity measures, and that unsupervised cross-lingual adaptation can be performed without explicit target knowledge [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. These methods are useful when the target data are scarce or unavailable in the target language, because they reuse a source language model and transfer its parameters to the target speaker or language.

Each method imposes different assumptions and constraints. Speaker adaptation assumes that a small amount of target speaker data can be sufficient to adjust the average model to the target speaker, while also relying on the source data to provide a robust prior [N1-F2]. Cross-lingual/state-mapping adaptation assumes that the source and target systems can be aligned at the state or model level, often using statistical similarity measures, and that the adaptation can transfer speaker characteristics across languages or speakers without requiring full target data [N6-R1][N6-R2]. These approaches are thus constrained by the quality and representativeness of the source data, by the alignment assumptions between source and target, and by the need for sufficient context to support parameter transformation [N1-F1][N6-R2].

Overall, the evidence supports a picture in which HMM adaptation under limited data uses speaker adaptation, state mapping, and related model-space transformations, with the main tradeoff being that the model can be tuned with small data, but only if the source data and alignment assumptions are strong enough to support the target change [N1-F1][N1-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2].
node_outputs.N10:
HMM adaptation techniques improve expressiveness by allowing the model to adjust spectral, excitation, duration, and prosodic parameters rather than relying only on a fixed speaker or style distribution [N1-F1]. The HTS paper explicitly states that voice characteristics, speaking styles, or emotions can be modified by transforming HMM parameters using adaptation [N1-F1]. The Persian speech synthesis paper shows that a small amount of speaker-specific data can produce high-quality synthetic speech that is close in quality to a speaker-dependent model trained on much more data [N1-F2]. This suggests that adaptation can preserve expressive quality while reducing the need for large target speaker datasets.

The expressive aspects being modeled or adjusted include prosody, speaking style, and emotional expression. The HTS overview notes that HMMs can model spectrum, excitation, and duration, and that the system can capture temporal structure [N1-F1]. The emotional speech synthesis survey emphasizes that emotional expression affects speech features such as spectral, prosodic, phonetic, ideolectal, and semantic aspects, and that synthesis systems typically take only a subset of these into account [N4-F3]. The HMM-based emotional synthesis literature also shows that HMM systems can be used to synthesize emotional speech and that average emotion models can be used to generate emotional speech [N4-R3][N4-R2]. In addition, the expressive speech synthesis literature indicates that HMM-based methods can support control over emotional expression intensity, speaking style, and prosody [N7-R3][N7-R5].

Adaptation supports speaker/style/prosody variation by shifting the model away from a single speaker or style. The HTS paper states that context-dependent HMMs can be trained from natural speech databases and that the system can generate speech with different styles without requiring very large databases [N1-F1]. The speaker adaptation paper shows that the average voice model is trained on multiple speakers, then transformed for a target speaker, enabling synthesis with arbitrary speaker characteristics [N1-F2]. The cross-lingual adaptation literature shows that state mapping can transfer speaker characteristics across languages or speakers, enabling variation without requiring full target data [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The expressive speech synthesis literature further indicates that adaptation and related methods can produce multiple emotion strengths and control speaking style intensity [N7-R2][N7-R5].

Limited data limits expressiveness because the model has less information to learn the target speaker’s style, prosody, or emotional characteristics. The Persian synthesis paper explicitly says that synthesizing speech with a small amount of data is essential because existing systems require large-scale corpora for multiple speakers [N1-F2]. The speaker adaptation paper explains that when available target speaker data are limited, adapting the average voice model becomes favorable [N1-F2]. In such cases, the model may not capture fine-grained variation if the target data are insufficient or too noisy. However, adaptation mitigates this by starting with a general-purpose model and fine-tuning it with minimal target data, so that the model can still produce plausible expressive speech even when training data are scarce [N1-F1][N1-F2].

In short, these techniques improve expressiveness by adjusting spectral/excitation/duration parameters and prosodic style, while speaker adaptation and cross-lingual/state-mapping adaptation allow variation across speakers, languages, or styles with limited target data [N1-F1][N1-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N4-F3][N7-R3][N7-R5].
node_outputs.N11:
The evidence suggests that for small-data settings, speaker adaptation and related model-space transformations are the most effective adaptation approaches, but they are not universally optimal and must be balanced against quality, expressiveness, and robustness. The HTS paper states that HMM-TTS systems are more flexible and can be adapted to mimic different speaking styles or speakers based on a limited amount of adaptation data [N5-F4]. The objective evaluation paper explicitly investigates how objective quality measures correlate with subjective performance in speaker-adaptive HMM-TTS systems and finds a reasonable correlation between several objective and subjective measures [N5-F4]. This implies that adaptation can be evaluated empirically, which is important for choosing the best approach when data are scarce.

The most effective adaptation approaches for small data appear to be those that can make the most efficient use of limited target data. Speaker adaptation is directly tied to small-data success because the Persian synthesis paper shows that a few target speaker utterances can produce high-quality speech comparable to a much larger speaker-dependent model [N1-F2]. Cross-lingual/state-mapping adaptation is also attractive for small data because it can transfer speaker characteristics from a source model to a target speaker or language without requiring large target data, and it can be performed unsupervised or with minimal explicit knowledge [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. These methods are therefore particularly useful when target data are scarce or unavailable.

However, there are clear tradeoffs. Quality can suffer if the adaptation is too weak or if the source model is not well aligned with the target. The objective evaluation paper notes that subjective listening tests are necessary to confirm how differences between adaptation methods are perceived and appreciated, while objective measures are useful for iterative tuning but less efficient for fine-grained comparison [N5-F4]. Expressiveness can also be limited if the adaptation does not capture the full target style or emotional variation. The expressive synthesis literature indicates that generating expressive speech with limited data can involve a trade-off between expressiveness and naturalness, and that systems can be designed to control that trade-off [N8-R2]. Robustness is another concern: the speaker adaptation paper emphasizes that the average voice model provides a priori information and a robust basis when target data are small, but it also implies that the quality depends on how well the source data represent the target speaker’s characteristics [N1-F2].

Performance is measured using both objective and subjective metrics. The objective evaluation paper uses mel-cepstral distance (MCD), frequency-weighted segmental SNR (FWS), cepstral distance (CEP), log-likelihood ratio (LLR), and weighted spectral slope (WSS), and it finds a reasonable correlation between several objective and subjective measures [N5-F4]. The same paper also investigates internal and output mel-cepstral distances, which are relevant because HMM synthesis depends on spectral and excitation parameters [N5-F4]. The expressive synthesis literature adds that performance in expressive synthesis is often evaluated by perceptual tests, and that some approaches explicitly aim to balance expressiveness against naturalness [N8-R2][N8-R3]. Taken together, the evidence indicates that the most effective adaptation approaches for small data are speaker adaptation and cross-lingual/state-mapping adaptation, but they are best chosen when objective and subjective measures align and when the target data are sufficient to support the desired expressive change [N5-F4][N1-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N8-R2].
node_outputs.N12:
HMM adaptation can still fail when data are very scarce because the model has insufficient information to learn the target speaker’s characteristics, prosody, or emotional expression. The Persian synthesis paper explicitly states that synthesizing speech with a small amount of data is essential because existing systems need large-scale corpora for multiple speakers, and that speaker adaptation makes speech with remarkable quality possible only when the speaker data are limited [N1-F2]. This implies that when data are extremely scarce, the adaptation may not be able to distinguish the target speaker from the source model or from noise, especially if the target data are noisy, few, or poorly representative [N1-F2]. The speaker adaptation literature also notes that speaker adaptation is used in recognition systems and later adopted for synthesis, but it is especially challenging when the target speaker’s data are sparse [N1-F2].

Prosody and emotion control can degrade under small-data conditions because the model may not learn the fine-grained variations required for expressive speech. The HTS overview says that HMMs can model spectrum, excitation, and duration, and that voice characteristics, speaking styles, or emotions can be modified by parameter transformation [N1-F1]. However, the emotional speech synthesis survey emphasizes that simulated emotional expression is typically well recognized when limited to exaggerated prototypical emotions, but that it is still difficult to capture natural, domain-independent expression [N4-F3]. The expressive speech synthesis literature similarly indicates that generating expressive pronunciations can be difficult with limited data, and that perceptual tests may show good-quality expressive samples but emotion-specific pronunciations may still be too limited [N7-R1]. This suggests that small data can support general expressive variation, but may not capture the precise prosodic or emotional details needed for high-quality synthesis.

Complementary approaches are needed to improve expressiveness when HMM adaptation alone is insufficient. The expressive synthesis literature points to distribution augmentation, controllable sequence-to-sequence architectures, and other data-augmentation techniques as ways to enhance expressive synthesis under limited training data [N8-R4][N8-R3]. When training data are limited, adaptation is not just a convenience—it becomes a core mechanism for creating expressive models. The evidence shows that HMM adaptation techniques are especially useful when target speaker data are scarce, because they can transfer a general-purpose model to the target speaker with only a small amount of adaptation data [N1-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2].

### 1) Which adaptation methods are commonly used in HMM speech synthesis?

The most common adaptation methods used in HMM speech synthesis are **speaker adaptation**, **cross-lingual/state-mapping adaptation**, and related model-space transformations. The HTS paper explicitly states that HMMs are used to model spectrum, excitation, and duration, and that voice characteristics, speaking styles, or emotions can be modified by transforming HMM parameters using techniques such as adaptation, interpolation, eigenvoice, or multiple regression [N1-F1]. In limited-data settings, speaker adaptation is particularly important because the Persian synthesis paper shows that a few target speaker utterances can produce high-quality synthetic speech comparable to a much larger speaker-dependent model [N1-F2]. Cross-lingual/state-mapping adaptation is also common, as it uses source-to-target state mapping or other alignment methods to transfer speaker characteristics across languages or speakers, and it can be performed unsupervised or with minimal explicit target knowledge [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

Each method imposes different assumptions and constraints. Speaker adaptation assumes that a small amount of target speaker data can be sufficient to adjust the average model to the target speaker, while also relying on the source data to provide a robust prior [N1-F2]. Cross-lingual/state-mapping adaptation assumes that the source and target systems can be aligned at the state or model level, often using statistical similarity measures, and that the adaptation can transfer speaker characteristics without requiring full target data [N6-R1][N6-R2]. These approaches are thus constrained by the quality and representativeness of the source data, by the alignment assumptions between source and target, and by the need for sufficient context to support parameter transformation [N1-F1][N6-R2].

The HTS paper says that voice characteristics, speaking styles, or emotions can be modified by transforming HMM parameters [N1-F1]. The HTS paper states that context-dependent HMMs can be trained from natural speech databases and that the system can generate speech with different styles without requiring very large databases [N1-F1]. The speaker adaptation paper shows that the average voice model is trained on multiple speakers, then transformed for a target speaker, enabling synthesis with arbitrary speaker characteristics [N1-F2]. The cross-lingual adaptation literature shows that state mapping can transfer speaker characteristics across languages or speakers, enabling variation without requiring full target data [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Limited data limits expressiveness because the model has less information to learn the target speaker’s style, prosody, or emotional characteristics. The Persian synthesis paper explicitly says that synthesizing speech with a small amount of data is essential because existing systems need large-scale corpora for multiple speakers [N1-F2]. Overall, HMM adaptation enables expressive speech synthesis with limited data by allowing the model to shift from a fixed speaker/style distribution to a more flexible, target-specific model using speaker adaptation, cross-lingual/state-mapping adaptation, and related transformations [N1-F1][N1-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2]. The best approach is therefore not a one-size-fits-all solution: speaker adaptation and cross-lingual/state-mapping adaptation are most effective when data are limited, but they should be chosen alongside objective and subjective evaluation and supplemented with augmentation or controllable architecture design to maximize expressiveness and robustness [N5-F4][N1-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N8-R2][N8-R4].
